answers.rationale: The user repeatedly states that Delta is preferred when it is comparable, while schedule and reliability override that preference only when materially better. Here every arrival works, A and B are both nonstop Main fares, and Delta is only $6 more; that is well within the user's demonstrated comparable-fare tolerance. The small savings or 10-minute earlier arrival on Alaska do not justify displacing the preferred carrier.

With the same hotel and rental window for all choices, the one-stop options add unnecessary failure points. Delta and Alaska are nearly equivalent nonstop choices, and the Delta premium is only $6. The user has repeatedly accepted modest Delta premiums when timing is effectively comparable and has said not to force Delta only when it worsens the routing; it does not do so here.

All nonstop arrivals are workable and seat details are explicitly deferred, so neither Southwest's lower fare nor American's 10-minute earlier arrival supplies a meaningful operational advantage. Delta costs only $5 more than American and $8 more than Southwest, making it the user's preferred-carrier choice at a comparable price and itinerary quality.

The fixed 4:15 p.m. materials desk is the operative constraint, and the user consistently protects hard event deadlines with real buffer rather than relying on a merely possible itinerary. C arrives at 12:35 p.m. and preserves substantial recovery time; A lands only 70 minutes before the desk, despite a connection and post-arrival ground steps. The user's Delta preference is explicitly subordinate to schedule reliability, so the United option with maximum cushion should lead.
